title: Embeddings dimension & batching + KV-cache on-prem latency SLO deep dive
summary: Deep technical review focused on embedding vector dimensionality, batching strategies, KV-cache implications for reranking, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Next steps: share benchmark template, schedule pilot run, follow up on security docs and on-prem deployment checklist.

quantization accuracy vs memory and throughput

transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Date: 2025-08-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 60 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood PM); Ravi Kapoor, Elena Martinez, Samir Patel (Kestrel)
Shared materials: link: drive.redwood/benchmarks-kestrel, link: drive.redwood/security-onprem.pdf

SUMMARY (auto):
Quick technical deep dive that got into vector dimensionality effects on retrieval + rerank, how KV-cache interacts with short lived re-rank queries, and quantization tradeoffs for on-prem nodes where memory is constrained. Action items and benchmark plan agreed.

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Maya: okay everyone thanks for joining, we want to focus on embeddings and rerank perf for the on-prem proof of concept, uh, coming from Kestrel. Ravi, do you want to kick off with what success looks like?
[00:18] Ravi: yeah thanks Maya. High level — we need sub-100ms p95 for a single-query rerank flow in the UI, that includes ANN lookup plus the rerank scoring across top-K (usually top-50). Cost matters because we're multi-tenant internally, and we have to fit within the existing GPU footprint.
[00:36] Elena: just to add, our current baseline uses 1536 dims embeddings stored in FAISS, we do an ANN recall then a BERT-like cross-encoder for rerank which is a huge cost; looking to move to a lightweight reranker using dense-similarity and small MLP to cut cost and latency.
[00:52] Liam: cool, so two knobs — embedding dim and reranker complexity. Also batching and KV-cache can change the p95 a lot. quick question — when you say p95 < 100ms, is that cold path or warm?
[01:06] Ravi: target is warm, i.e., normal traffic with some cache warm. Cold can be higher.
[01:12] Priya: noted. we'll scope warm-path first, but also capture cold warm-up behavior in the benchmarks.
[01:20] Maya: great. let's walk matrix: dims — 128, 512, 1536 (your current), maybe 2048 if you consider future models. batch sizes — 1 (interactive), 8, 64 (throughput). quant profiles — fp16, int8, 4-bit symmetric/async. and KV-cache — eviction/timestamp TTLs and prefix cache helpful for long chats but for quick search rerank KV behavior is different.
[01:44] Elena: i worry about accuracy loss if we drop dims to 512 or 128. Our offline eval shows small drop at 512, bigger at 128 for recall@10.
[01:54] Liam: that's expected. small vectors reduce representational capacity; the UX tradeoff depends on how much rerank you're doing vs ANN recall. one pattern: keep higher dim for index (1536) but store compact reranker inputs — or pre-filter with ANN then run reranking on smaller embedding projection.
[02:12] [02:12] Samir: so how does KV-cache factor in? for rerank we often re-run similar queries with minor changes. Will KV-cache actually hit?
[02:21] Liam: good question. KV-cache in generation runtimes caches key-value for autoregressive decoding; for embedding/rerank flows it's a different cache — think of an embedding prefix cache or a feature cache. Redwood supports prefix and kv-like caches for both text and feature vectors at the platform layer, but naming is sometimes off in transcriptions so we'll call it feature cache. For rerank, if your top-K set is stable across subsequent queries, we can cache reranker inputs and small MLP outputs to avoid recomputing.
[02:49] Elena: oh interesting — so store the top-50 candidate embeddings or their reduced projections to reuse? that could help.
[02:56] Maya: exactly. store projection to 128-dim for reranker step; that reduces compute and memory in the rerank stage. But careful with staleness and eviction TTLs.
[03:06] Ravi: what's the memory cost at different dims — rough numbers?
[03:10] Liam: rough: 1536 dims float32 ~ 6 KB per vector (1536*4 bytes ≈ 6144 bytes). 512 dims float32 ~ 2 KB. In int8 it's ~1.5 KB for 1536 (packed). 4-bit quant halves that. So index size and RAM for embeddings scales linearly. ANN index (FAISS ivf+pq) changes those numbers a bit.
[03:34] Elena: does Redwood provide on-node quantization helpers or do we need to run external quant?
[03:39] Maya: Redwood Optimize includes quant suggestions and automated flows for common models; for on-prem we'll provide the quantization recipes and scripts. Liam can show the runbook.
[03:47] Liam: yep, we have a runbook. two caveats: 1) 4-bit quant may introduce vector retrieval noise leading to recall loss, 2) int8 with per-channel calibration keeps most of the cosine order but you must evaluate post-quant similarity. We'll add example microbenchmarks in the sheet.
[04:06] Priya: note: on-prem constraints — network egress isn't an issue but service accounts, KMS and HSM for secret management are. We'll include the security checklist.
[04:15] Samir: for our on-prem we have 8xA100 equivalent splinter nodes; would that be enough for production rerank at our traffic (peak 1200 QPS)?
[04:25] Liam: depends on batch sizing. If you run interactive single-query (batch=1) at p95 < 100ms we'll need X GPUs — approximations: a single A100 can do ~500 sents/s for small MLP reranker at batch=8, but those numbers vary with kernel selection and quantization. For batch=64 throughput mode, you get better GPU amortization but increased per-request latency (queueing).
[04:49] Elena: can we approximate cost? memory + GPU hours?
[04:53] Maya: we'll produce a cost-per-1M-queries estimate in the spreadsheet after you run the benchmarks and we model scheduling (dedicated vs shared). For Dedicated reserved pools we can price predictably; on-prem case is internal cost allocation.
[05:05] Ravi: curious about ANN layer — you recommended keeping index at higher dim and projecting for reranker. How does that interact with index size and recall?
[05:14] Liam: typical pattern: index and ANN operate on original embeddings (1536) for recall accuracy. For rerank, create a learned projection to 128 or 256 dims that preserves ordering for candidate set. The projection model is much smaller and cheaper to run. You'll measure small hit to final accuracy vs full cross-encoder but huge latency wins.
[05:34] Elena: any caveats with cosine vs dot product if we quantize?
[05:38] Liam: quantization changes scale; per-vector normalization before quantization helps preserve cosine semantics. We often do L2-normalize then quantize. Also use per-channel scale for int8 to keep distances stable.
[05:50] [05:50] Maya: let's talk SLA mapping — you said p95 target warm of <100ms. We'll break down components: ANN lookup (FAISS) 10-40ms, projection & rerank compute 20-60ms depending on batch/quant, network + serialization 5-20ms. The sums must be <100ms. If we need headroom we push for batch=1 optimized kernels and int8 with warm cache.
[06:14] Samir: what about cold cache — loading index shards on demand could spike latency; can Redwood pin shards on nodes?
[06:22] Liam: Yes — for Private deployments we can pin index shards and pre-warm caches. There's an orchestration option to keep top-k shards resident or to use a cold-start grace period with fallback to a smaller index. We'll document orchestration flags.
[06:36] Elena: for ANN we use IVF-PQ with 16 bytes per vector post-PQ, does that map to the quant numbers you gave?
[06:42] Liam: that lines up; PQ compresses vectors and reduces memory massively at cost of recall. A hybrid approach: keep a coarse IVF for recall then fetch raw or high-fidelity vectors for rerank when needed.
[06:54] Ravi: are there Redwood features that do automatic routing to cheaper models when load spikes? e.g., fall back to 512-dim model?
[07:02] Maya: yes, smart routing can route to cheaper model variants or regions based on policy. It can also do graceful degradation: route non-SLA requests to lower-cost cluster, keep premium traffic on dedicated pool.
[07:14] Priya: for the bench matrix, we'll capture: recall@10, mrr@10, p50/p95/p99 latency for ANN+rerank combined, GPU utilization, and memory footprint. Also note the quant-induced accuracy delta column.
[07:28] Liam: we'll instrument token-level (here vector-level) breakdown for each run. Expect variance; we recommend at least 3 runs per configuration to median heavy tails.
[07:36] Elena: small practical Q — we often do rerank for top-150 then trim to 50; what's the CPU/GPU work cost there?
[07:43] Liam: linear in candidates; 150 rerank on small MLP is heavier but still much cheaper than cross-encoder. For MLP with 2 layers and projection to 128 it is microseconds per vector on GPU if batched well. The overhead is memory copy and kernel launch — batching avoids repeated launches.
[07:58] Maya: kernel launch overhead is what makes batch=1 expensive; we can use persistent kernels and low-latency launches in our runtime for these microjobs. That is one of Redwood's optimizations.
[08:08] Samir: if we go with quantized int8 on on-prem, are you able to provide the calibration tools? we can't risk production data leakage during calibration.
[08:17] Liam: yes, we have a privacy-preserving calibration path — run calibration on sampled synthetic or anonymized vectors. We'll provide scripts that run in your VPC; no data leaves the cluster.
[08:28] Elena: ok good. also need to validate our ANN implementation interacts well with Redwood's feature cache—i've seen mismatches before.
[08:35] Liam: we'll include integration tests in the runbook. Expect to run small smoke tests for consistency of distances pre/post-quant/index load.
[08:44] Maya: any blockers from Kestrel side?
[08:47] Ravi: we need the benchmark sheet and the security docs; Samir will create access once Maya requests. Also timeline: we want pilot live in Sept if possible.
[08:58] Maya: sounds doable. we'll target data collection and pilot config by end of August.
[09:03] Priya: last note — for on-prem we recommend starting with int8 per-channel quant on 1536 then evaluate projection to 256/128. That reduces memory and keeps high recall.
[09:13] Elena: thanks we'll try that.
[09:16] Maya: recap of next steps — Maya send sheet and docs, Liam send quant runbook + run commands, Samir set up infra access, Elena run bench and upload. follow-up call week of Aug 25. Anything else?
[09:30] Ravi: not from me. thanks everyone.
[09:33] Maya: thanks all.

END OF TRANSCRIPT

NOTES: transcript has occasional mistranscriptions of product names (e.g., "face" for FAISS) and generic speaker labeling in recording. Links referenced: drive.redwood/benchmarks-kestrel, drive.redwood/security-onprem.pdf, runbook.redwood/quant-runbook-v2.pdf
